newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Rao wins breathing space in forgery case.
newsitem.headline: India's Rao wins breathing space in forgery case.

text.p: Former Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao won temporary legal protection from arrest on Wednesday in a criminal forgery case that has jolted the nation's political system and stock markets.
Delhi High Court Judge S.K. Mahajan granted Rao pre-emptive, or anticipatory, bail until a lower court holds a hearing into the seven-year-old case next Monday.
The ruling gave some breathing space to Rao, who is under legal pressure in two separate cases.

But while Rao won limited respite from the threat of arrest, it seemed all but certain that next week he would become the first former prime minister to appear in court to face criminal charges and, possibly, arrest.

Rao, who served as prime minister from mid-1991 until last May when his Congress party, hobbled by allegations of corruption, was defeated in polls, was expected to be detained when he appears at next Monday's hearing in the forgery case.

Judge Mahajan said Rao could apply for ordinary bail at the October 14 session, when he was scheduled to be formally charged with forgery and two other counts carrying a maximum sentence of seven years in jail.
If denied bail, Rao would be put in custody pending trial. Newspapers said a local hospital had prepared a room for Rao, who suffers from diabetes and heart trouble.
Rao's lawyers said they planned to lodge an appeal with the Supreme Court against the Delhi High Court ruling, seeking indefinite legal protection against arrest for their client.

Rao quit as head of India's oldest party last month after a judge upheld a summons ordering him to appear in court in a separate criminal cheating case. Rao says he is innocent of allegations he helped cheat a businessman of $100,000 in 1983.

The former Congress party chief had been scheduled to appear in court last week in the cheating case, but the Supreme Court intervened by taking up a police request to shift the venue of the hearing from a crowded local court to a safer location.
The Supreme Court was expected to rule on the request this week. On Wednesday, the lower court judge rescheduled the cheating hearing for October 16.
Rao's legal troubles have shaken the fragile political balance that resulted from May's inconclusive poll.
Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's minority government depends on Congress to weather a potential parliamentary challenge by the opposition Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Before he quit as Congress leader, Rao pledged support to Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition, saying his party wanted above all to prevent the right-wing BJP from taking power.
Congress and Deve Gowda's United Front claim the BJP, which draws its strength from India's Hindu majority, is a divisive force. The BJP says India is united by a single, Hindu culture.

But Congress's new leader, Sitaram Kesri, has threatened to withdraw his party's support for Deve Gowda if the United Front coalition does not back a Congress alliance in Uttar Pradesh, the most populous state and biggest regional political prize.

The rumblings of discontent between Congress and the United Front have helped trigger a sell-off in stock markets, which fear a period of political uncertainty could slow the pace of economic reform and discourage foreign investment.
Rao's forgery case dates from 1989. Federal police charged the former prime minister and five others with using false documents to defame a rival politician.
